title: The Case of the Missing Glow
markdown:
Samir’s workshop usually hummed with gadgets and enthusiasm. His latest creation — a slime so dazzling it practically glowed — was meant for the library STEM fair. Electric green. Wisp, his ferret, was usually a furry tornado. Today: silence. A heavy, worried silence. The slime sat in its jar, a sad greyish puddle, brilliance gone. Forgotten pond scum.

“What’s happening, Wisp?” Samir’s brow made a tiny canyon. He nudged the jar. No spark. Wisp, normally first to investigate, only twitched a weary ear. Bright eyes half-closed. Usual spark extinguished.

The door creaked. Sunlight, and Engineer Mara, concern on a face that preferred cheer. Her hands, usually busy with tools, were clasped. “Samir. A problem. A peculiar one.” She held out a small metallic component. The plating on her new gravity stabilizers — built for an experimental hover-scooter — looked muted, as if fine dust had settled for good. “Losing its sheen. Turning dull. Quickly.”

Samir turned the piece in his fingers. Not just his slime. Mara’s invention too. “Something’s leaching the sparkle out of everything.” Wisp managed a small sad sigh, as if he agreed and charged consulting fees in yawns.

Samir’s brain was already digging. Mr. Abernathy, science, chromatography: separating things into their true colours, even things you cannot see. He grabbed a roll of plain coffee filters, the kind that made a decent cuppa.

With the speed of a tiny surgeon he tore off a strip, set a blob of dull slime in the centre, added a single drop of water. The first strip bloomed too fast and ran off the edge, a mess. He started again, smaller drop, flatter table. The water wicked outward, carrying pigments. Faint trails of colour. He repeated the process with grey workshop dust swept from the windowsill — not the floor, where too many other stories lived — then with a scraping Mara had taken from the dull stabilizer. Wisp sat on the kettle and judged the waiting.

“Watch.” Three filters. Three miniature landscapes. The slime showed faint bands of original green and yellow — and a surprising dull greyish-brown streak. The dust filter had a similar greyish-brown streak, almost identical. Mara’s sample: another identical band.

“Same dulling agent.” His voice found its buzz again. “This band. Identical in all three. Same stuff. Slime, dust, metal.”

He scanned the workshop. On the far side, Pipkin Spark — another young tinkerer with a habit of borrowing ideas — had recently installed a new exhaust fan. Yesterday Pipkin had boasted it was super-powered and eco-friendly, which in Pipkin’s mouth usually meant cheap and loud.

“Pipkin,” Samir called, sharp and clear. “What filter did you put on that fan?”

Pipkin, humming off-key, jumped. Smirk wavering. “A really good one. Super efficient. The best.” He would not meet Samir’s eye. A wrench clanged. The faint acrid smell of cheap plastic from the fan seemed to enjoy the moment.

Samir walked over, boots crunching. He examined the fan, then the exhaust port. “Efficient? The mesh is torn. I bet it’s spewing this.” He held up a vial of fine grey dust collected near the housing. “A contaminant. Reacts with phosphorescent materials and polished metals. Steals shine and glow. Your filter is poisoning the air. My slime and Mara’s stabilizers are the latest victims.”

Pipkin’s grin vanished. Pale. Guilty. “I didn’t mean to. I just wanted it to be better than yours.”

Mara stepped in, stern and fair. “Intentions are one thing. Consequences are another.” She glanced at the three filters, then at Samir. “Chromatography. You separated what the eye called grey into a fingerprint. Same band, three places. That’s the proof, not the shouting.”

Samir grinned, just a little. “A fingerprint for the muck.”

They washed the dust. They fixed the fan. Pipkin, under Samir and Mara’s supervision, installed a proper filter that did not pretend to be heroic. Wisp, feeling the air clear, regained his bounce and chased a dust bunny with professional interest. The slime, given a clean jar and a night, remembered a hint of green.

Samir pegged the three filters to the pegboard, labelled, in case anyone wanted to argue later. He did not announce that the world was full of wonderful puzzles. He made tea with the rest of the roll, because the filters had done enough detective work for one afternoon, and Wisp stole a biscuit crumb with his old, unextinguished spark.
